resolutions.finding: C1: R008 says unsentSessionID holds back the session ID until the first message goes through; critic says the API-key branch contradicts this.
resolutions.truth: SOURCE FACT. Two disjoint session-start branches exist in ThreadRuntime.ensureSession (DroppyCode/App/Runtime/ThreadRuntime.swift:1394-1569). The API-key branch ends at ThreadRuntime.swift:1488-1491: `guard session === candidate, !Task.isCancelled else { throw CancellationError() }` / `started = true` / `app.updateThread(threadID) { $0.providerSessionID = sessionID }` / `return candidate`. It writes providerSessionID DIRECTLY and never calls recordSessionID. The CLI branch ends at ThreadRuntime.swift:1565-1568 with `recordSessionID(sessionID)`. recordSessionID (ThreadRuntime.swift:1574-1581) is: `guard let app else { return }` / `if app.thread(threadID)?.providerSessionID == nil { unsentSessionID = sessionID } else { app.updateThread(threadID) { $0.providerSessionID = sessionID } }`. The only other writer of unsentSessionID is the `.sessionReady` handler at ThreadRuntime.swift:2081-2082 (`case .sessionReady(let sessionID): recordSessionID(sessionID)`). unsentSessionID is declared at ThreadRuntime.swift:423, promoted to the thread only inside the post-send block at ThreadRuntime.swift:1336-1339, and cleared in releaseSession at ThreadRuntime.swift:2045. Full grep of the file for `unsentSessionID` yields exactly lines 423, 1336, 1337, 1338, 1577, 2045 plus the doc comment at 1572. SOURCE FACT: the API-key providers (.deepseek, .meta, .zai, per Provider.swift:95 `var isAPIKeyBased: Bool { self == .deepseek || self == .meta || self == .zai }`) also never emit `.sessionReady` - grep of DroppyCode/Services/Providers/ for `onEvent?(.exited` and for `.sessionReady` shows OpenAICompatibleSession.swift (the base for DeepSeekSession/MetaSession/ZaiSession) emits neither; its start() simply returns the id (OpenAICompatibleSession.swift:247-265). So for API providers the hold-back mechanism is entirely absent, by both routes.
resolutions.port_impact: The Windows port must keep two separate ID-recording paths. CLI/ACP providers: hold the id in an in-memory `unsentSessionID` and only write it to the thread after a successful send (ThreadRuntime.swift:1336-1339) or when the thread already has a providerSessionID. API-key providers: write providerSessionID unconditionally the moment start() returns. Do not unify them.

resolutions.finding: C3: R033 says SimpleDiff's 200_000 cap is the same cap that bounds ThreadRuntime.fileEdits; critic says two separate constants with different operands.
resolutions.truth: SOURCE FACT. Two independent constants, both literally 200_000, applied to different operands. (1) DroppyCode/Core/Support/Text.swift:81 `static let diffLimit = 200_000`, used once at Text.swift:101: `guard old.utf8.count + new.utf8.count <= diffLimit else { return FileEdit.Stats(diff: nil, additions: added.count, deletions: removed.count) }` - it bounds the sum of the two INPUT texts. (2) DroppyCode/App/Runtime/ThreadRuntime.swift:3366 `private nonisolated static let editDiffLimit = 200_000`, used twice: ThreadRuntime.swift:3373 `guard let diff = edit.diff, diff.utf8.count > editDiffLimit else { return edit }` (inside `capped(_:)`, which nils out an oversized provider-reported patch), and ThreadRuntime.swift:3397 `let diff = section.utf8.count <= editDiffLimit ? section : nil` (inside `fileEdits(from:repositoryRoot:)`, per-file section of a git patch). Both bound the PRODUCED hunk. R033 is not inventing the conflation: it is repeating the source's own comments, which say so twice and are themselves imprecise - Text.swift:80 'The same cap bounds command diffs (`ThreadRuntime.fileEdits`).' and ThreadRuntime.swift:3370 'The same cap the edits taken from a command's diff have.' ENGINEERING DECISION: the comments are wrong about the operand, not about the number.
resolutions.port_impact: Define both constants (or one shared 200000 with two distinct call sites) and apply them to the correct operands: input-size gate on the SimpleDiff producer, output-size gate on both ThreadRuntime edit cappers. A single gate on one operand changes which edits keep their hunk.

resolutions.finding: G2: The API-key and CLI session-start paths differ in three unreported ways.
resolutions.truth:
Three sub-claims, adjudicated separately against ThreadRuntime.swift:1430-1492 (API) and 1494-1568 (CLI).
(a) PARTLY RIGHT. SOURCE FACT: `isStartingSession = true` appears exactly once, at ThreadRuntime.swift:1534, inside the CLI branch, and is reset at 1536 in that branch's `defer`. The API branch's defer (1467-1476) does not touch it. Grep of the whole file for `isStartingSession` returns only lines 444 (declaration `@ObservationIgnored private var isStartingSession = false`), 1534, 1536 and 2172. So the flag asymmetry is real. BUT the consequence the critic draws is UNREACHABLE: the `.exited` event is emitted only by process-backed sessions - a whole-tree grep for `onEvent?(.exited` hits ACPSession.swift:630, AntigravitySession.swift:379, ClaudeSession.swift:685, CodexSession.swift:1019, CopilotSession.swift:940, PiSession.swift:648 and :651, and nothing in OpenAICompatibleSession.swift / DeepSeekSession.swift / MetaSession.swift / ZaiSession.swift. An API-key session has no process and never emits `.exited`, so the missing guard can never fire for it.
(b) CORRECT - see resolution C1 above; same evidence.
(c) CORRECT and then some. SOURCE FACT: the API retry predicate is the inline catch clause at ThreadRuntime.swift:1479 `} catch where thread.providerSessionID != nil && thread.providerResumeAt == nil && allowNewSession && session === candidate && !Task.isCancelled {`, whose body (1482-1486) is `releaseSession(stop: true)` / `candidate = makeAPISession(resumeID: nil)` / `session = candidate` / `sessionSignature = signature` / `sessionID = try await candidate.start()`. It emits no notice and never clears providerResumeAt. The CLI catch at 1548 is `} catch where allowNewSession && session === candidate && !Task.isCancelled && Self.startsOver(after: error, resuming: thread) {` with body 1553-1563: `releaseSession(stop: true)` / `if Self.lostConversation(error) { app.updateThread(threadID) { $0.providerResumeAt = nil }; if currentTurnID != nil { appendNotice(.warning, "\(thread.provider.displayName) no longer has this conversation. It starts a new one here, without the messages above.") } }` / makeSession(resumeID: nil) / reassign / start(). Helpers: `startsOver(after:resuming:)` at 1586-1589 is `guard thread.providerSessionID != nil else { return false }; return lostConversation(error) || thread.providerResumeAt == nil`; `lostConversation(_:)` at 1593-1597 is `let text = error.localizedDescription; return text.localizedCaseInsensitiveContains("no conversation found") || text.localizedCaseInsensitiveContains("no longer has this conversation")`. ADDITIONAL SOURCE FACT the critic missed: the API retry arm is effectively UNREACHABLE. `OpenAICompatibleSession.start()` (OpenAICompatibleSession.swift:247-265) has exactly one throw site, line 248 `guard !apiKey.isEmpty else { throw ProviderError.notInstalled(config.kind) }`, and ThreadRuntime.swift:1431-1433 already refuses to build the session when `app.settings.apiKey(for: thread.provider).isEmpty`. Lines 249-264 do no I/O and cannot throw. So start() on an API session cannot throw once the branch is entered, and the 1479 catch never runs.
resolutions.port_impact: Reproduce both branches separately. The API branch: no start-guard flag, direct providerSessionID write, no lost-conversation notice, no providerResumeAt clearing, and a retry arm that in practice never fires. The CLI branch: set the start-guard flag across start(), route the id through the hold-back, and on a lost conversation clear providerResumeAt and emit the exact warning string above. Port the two contains() probes as case-insensitive substring tests on the error's message - on Windows that means the message text the CLI writes, not an OS error code.

resolutions.finding: G3: The API session factory's `default: DeepSeekSession(configuration:)` arm is unreachable and R008 classifies nothing as unreachable.
resolutions.truth: SOURCE FACT. ThreadRuntime.swift:1453-1458: `let created: any ProviderSession = switch thread.provider { case .deepseek: DeepSeekSession(configuration: configuration) / case .meta: MetaSession(configuration: configuration) / case .zai: ZaiSession(configuration: configuration) / default: DeepSeekSession(configuration: configuration) }`. The enclosing branch is entered only under `if thread.provider.isAPIKeyBased` (ThreadRuntime.swift:1430), and Provider.swift:95 defines `var isAPIKeyBased: Bool { self == .deepseek || self == .meta || self == .zai }`. ProviderKind (Provider.swift:3-16) has exactly 13 cases: codex, claude, cursor, opencode, grok, deepseek, meta, zai, devin, antigravity, copilot, commandcode, pi. ENGINEERING DECISION on classification: the arm is RUNTIME-UNREACHABLE but COMPILER-REQUIRED - the switch lists 3 of 13 enum cases, so Swift needs a default for exhaustiveness. It is not dead code the compiler prunes; it is a required fall-through that no input reaches. Contrast the CLI factory at ThreadRuntime.swift:1513-1524, which enumerates all 13 cases and has no default.
resolutions.port_impact: In the port, write the API factory as an exhaustive 3-way dispatch with an unreachable fallback (assert/throw or mirror the DeepSeek choice). Do not treat the default arm as a supported path for a fourth API provider - adding one requires editing Provider.isAPIKeyBased, and the fallback would silently mis-instantiate it as DeepSeek.

resolutions.finding: G5: interrupt() has a distinct .starting fast path that never calls session.interrupt() and never arms the watchdog.
resolutions.truth: SOURCE FACT. ThreadRuntime.swift:1655-1683. `func interrupt() {` / 1656 `guard phase != .idle else { return }` / 1657 `let turnID = currentTurnID` / 1658-1659 `interruptWatchdog?.cancel(); interruptWatchdog = nil` / 1664-1668 `if phase == .starting { currentTurnID = nil; Task { await finishTurn(status: .interrupted, turnID: turnID) }; return }` / 1669-1676 `Task { guard currentTurnID == turnID, turnID != nil else { return }; if let session { await session.interrupt() } else { await finishTurn(status: .interrupted, turnID: turnID) } }` / 1677-1682 `interruptWatchdog = Task { [weak self] in try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(8)); guard let self, !Task.isCancelled, self.currentTurnID == turnID, turnID != nil else { return }; self.releaseSession(stop: true); await self.finishTurn(status: .interrupted) }`. The source's own comment (1660-1663) states the intent: nothing has been sent yet, so the provider has no turn to stop and the watchdog would kill a session that is only just starting; the message it was about to send never goes. Note the watchdog's final finishTurn at 1681 passes NO turnID, unlike the .starting path and the inner Task.
resolutions.port_impact: Port three distinct interrupt behaviours: (1) idle -> no-op; (2) .starting -> clear currentTurnID, finish as .interrupted, drop the pending message, no provider call, no watchdog; (3) .running -> ask the session to interrupt and arm an 8 second watchdog that force-releases the session. The 8 seconds is a literal, not a tunable.

resolutions.finding: G6: resolve(_:option:) also mutates ProposedPlan.state before forwarding; unreported.
resolutions.truth: SOURCE FACT. ThreadRuntime.swift:1685-1695: `func resolve(_ request: ApprovalRequest, option: ApprovalRequest.Option) { approvals.removeAll { $0.id == request.id } / if request.kind == .plan, let itemID = request.toolItemID, let entry = entryIndex[itemID], case .plan(var plan) = entry.item.content { plan.state = option.role == .approve ? .accepted : .dismissed; entry.item.content = .plan(plan); saveRevision += 1; scheduleSave() } / session?.resolveApproval(request.id, optionID: option.id) }`. Order matters: the approval is removed from the in-memory list FIRST, the persisted plan state is written SECOND, and the provider is told LAST. The sibling `answer(_:answers:)` (1697-1700) has no such mutation: `questions.removeAll { $0.id == request.id }; session?.answerQuestion(request.id, answers: answers)`. Related: `dismissPlan(_:)` at 1132-1138 sets `plan.state = .dismissed`, bumps saveRevision and calls scheduleSave, with no provider call at all.
resolutions.port_impact: Port resolve() with the persisted plan-state write in the middle, gated on all four conditions (kind == .plan, non-nil toolItemID, the item exists in the index, and its content is a plan). Any approve-role option accepts the plan; every other role dismisses it.

resolutions.finding: G7: startTurn silently converts a send into a queued follow-up in three cases.
resolutions.truth: SOURCE FACT, and there is a fourth exit the critic missed. ThreadRuntime.swift:1158-1167: `private func startTurn(text: String, attachments: [Attachment], hydraHeads: [Int]? = nil, hydraBrief: Bool = false) async {` / 1159-1162 `guard phase == .idle, !isReverting else { enqueueFollowUp(text: text, attachments: attachments); return }` / 1163 `guard let app, let initialThread = app.thread(threadID), let project = app.project(initialThread.projectID) else { return }` / 1164-1167 `guard !initialThread.isArchived else { enqueueFollowUp(text: text, attachments: attachments); return }`. So there are THREE enqueueing exits (phase != .idle, isReverting, thread.isArchived) and ONE SILENT DROP at 1163 when the app, the thread or its project is missing - that path enqueues nothing and the message is lost. Also SOURCE FACT: the enqueue calls pass only text and attachments, so `hydraHeads` and `hydraBrief` are DISCARDED on every deferral - a head's report or a lead's brief deferred this way comes back as a plain user bubble.
resolutions.port_impact: Port all four exits. Treat the hydraHeads/hydraBrief loss on deferral as upstream behaviour to reproduce, not to fix (see upstream defects).

resolutions.finding: G8: warmSession clears warmup only on success or on the phase re-check; a throwing ensureSession disables warm starts for the process.
resolutions.truth: SOURCE FACT. ThreadRuntime.swift:1380-1392: `func warmSession() {` / 1381-1383 `guard phase == .idle, session == nil, warmup == nil, !isReverting, let app, let thread = app.thread(threadID), !thread.isArchived, !thread.provider.isAPIKeyBased, let project = app.project(thread.projectID) else { return }` / 1384 `let directory = thread.worktreePath ?? project.path` / 1385-1391 `warmup = Task { [weak self] in guard let self else { return }; await ensureModel(thread); guard phase == .idle, session == nil else { warmup = nil; return }; if (try? await ensureSession(directory: directory)) != nil { warmup = nil } }`. A whole-file grep for `warmup` returns exactly lines 416 (declaration), 1247, 1381, 1385, 1388, 1390 - there is no other assignment. So a throwing ensureSession leaves `warmup` holding a finished Task forever, and the `warmup == nil` precondition at 1381 then refuses every subsequent warm start for the life of that runtime instance. The source comment at 1389 states the intent: 'A start that fails is not retried on every keystroke: the send makes its own.' The lingering handle is harmless to sends: ThreadRuntime.swift:1247 `if let warmup { await warmup.value }` returns immediately for a completed task. Note also the guard excludes API-key providers entirely (1382), so warm starts are CLI/ACP only.
resolutions.port_impact: Reproduce the sticky latch. Do not add a reset on failure and do not reset it when the runtime is reused - the latch is per-runtime-instance and is deliberately never cleared after a failed start. A port that clears it will hammer a broken CLI on every keystroke.

resolutions.finding: G9: discardThreadState teardown ordering is unreported, and its cancelPersistence-before-stopSession is the opposite of releaseIdleRuntime's saveNow-then-cancelPersistence.
resolutions.truth: SOURCE FACT, with the mechanism the critic did not name. DroppyCode/App/AppModel.swift:1070-1077: `private func discardThreadState(_ thread: ChatThread, deletingDocument: Bool = true) { idleSessionStops.removeValue(forKey: thread.id)?.cancel() / runtimes[thread.id]?.cancelPersistence() / runtimes[thread.id]?.stopSession() / runtimes[thread.id] = nil / terminals.closeAll(for: thread.id) / if deletingDocument { Storage.deleteDocument(thread.id) } }`. AppModel.swift:493-506: `func releaseIdleRuntime(_ id: UUID) -> Bool { guard let runtime = runtimes[id], selectedThreadID != id, let thread = thread(id), thread.parentThreadID == nil || thread.parentThreadID != selectedThreadID, runtime.holdsOnlyPersistedState, !sessionsToRelease.contains(id), autoContinue.resumesAt[id] == nil, terminals.sessions(for: id).isEmpty, runningDroppyHeads(of: id) == 0 else { return false } / runtime.saveNow() / runtime.cancelPersistence() / runtimes[id] = nil / return true }` - eight guard conditions, counted. THE MECHANISM: `cancelPersistence()` (ThreadRuntime.swift:3522-3528) sets `persistenceEnabled = false` and cancels saveTask and flushTask; `stopSession()` (ThreadRuntime.swift:2058-2075) calls `saveNow()` at line 2068; and `saveNow()` (3484-3498) begins `saveTask?.cancel(); saveTask = nil; guard persistenceEnabled, !isLoadingHistory else { return }`. So calling cancelPersistence FIRST deliberately neuters the save that stopSession would otherwise perform. That is intentional, because all three callers of discardThreadState are delete paths: AppModel.swift:560 (removeProject, every thread of the project), :944 (delete, after helpers and the hydra-head stop), and :976 (deleteArchivedThreads, with deletingDocument: false followed by a batched `Storage.deleteDocuments(removed.map(\.id))` at :981).
resolutions.port_impact: Port both orders literally and port the persistenceEnabled latch, because the ordering only has meaning through that latch. Delete path: disable persistence, then stop the session (whose internal save is now a no-op), then drop the runtime, close terminals, delete the document. Idle-release path: save synchronously, then disable persistence, then drop the runtime - and gate it behind all eight conditions, including the autoContinue wait and the running-head count.

resolutions.finding: CC8: RecentCache is generational, not LRU; every cache in this family is one of these and reports describe them by limit alone.
resolutions.truth: SOURCE FACT. DroppyCode/Core/Support/RecentCache.swift, 57 lines, full behaviour: two maps `current` and `previous` with `currentCost`/`previousCost` (9-12); `init(limit:costLimit:)` clamps `limit = max(1, limit)` and `costLimit = max(0, costLimit)` (17-18), costLimit defaulting to `.max` (16). `value(for:)` (22-28): a `current` hit returns without mutating; a `previous` hit is REMOVED from previous, its cost subtracted, and re-inserted into current - so a read that lands in the old generation is mutating. `contains(_:)` (30-32) checks both maps and does NOT promote. `insert(_:for:cost:)` (43-56): `removeValue(for: key)` first, then `guard cost <= costLimit else { return }`, then the rollover `if current.count >= limit || currentCost > costLimit - cost { previous = current; previousCost = currentCost; current = [:]; current.reserveCapacity(limit); currentCost = 0 }`, then store. The whole current map becomes previous in one step, so effective findable capacity is up to 2x limit and eviction is by generation, not recency. Instantiations across the tree, 17 counted: ThreadRuntime.swift:198 and :1921 revisionDiffs(limit 4), :1920 turnDiffs(limit 64); HydraButton.swift:144 delegationChecks(32); TimelineMinimap.swift:39 entryCache(400); TimelineRows.swift:776 readingCache(200) and :2185 cache(60); ComposerView.swift:1125 built(2); ThumbnailCache.swift:16 thumbnails(120, 32 MB) and :70 images(120, 16 MB); Storage.swift:270 DocumentPrefetch.ready via `init(limit: Int = 12, costLimit: Int = 16 * 1_024 * 1_024, pendingLimit: Int = 24, ...)` at Storage.swift:264-273; AttachmentPreview.swift:22 resolvedPaths(600); Components.swift:19 days(256); MarkdownView.swift:107 blockCache(800), :563 prettyCache(1200), :1348 cellCache(1200).
resolutions.port_impact: Implement the generational cache exactly; an LRU substitute changes both hit rate and memory ceiling. Carry the 17 limits and the two cost limits verbatim. Note the read-promotes-and-mutates contract when choosing a thread-safe container on Windows: `value(for:)` needs write access.

resolutions.finding: CC9: Em-dash flattening happens on at least three passes and a port that implements it once will double-clean or miss.
resolutions.truth: The inventory is right and incomplete; the 'double-clean' hazard is WRONG. SOURCE FACT, all 7 call sites, from a whole-tree grep for withoutEmDashes/cleanedOfEmDashes: Storage.swift:79 `document.items = document.items.filter { !$0.isEmptyReasoning }.map(\.cleanedOfEmDashes)` on every read; ThreadRuntime.swift:562 `let loaded = document.items.filter { !$0.isEmptyReasoning }.map { TimelineEntry($0.cleanedOfEmDashes) }` at install; ThreadRuntime.swift:2966 `let prose = kind == .toolOutput ? text : TextCleanup.withoutEmDashes(text)` on every streamed delta except tool output; ThreadRuntime.swift:3097 (completeMessage), :3117 (completeReasoning), :3135 (completePlan); and ThreadRuntime.swift:2158 on a provider-supplied title. `cleanedOfEmDashes` (Timeline.swift:38-54) rewrites only `.assistant` message text, `.reasoning` block text and `.plan` markdown, with `default: break` - user text, tool output and notices are untouched. The replacement set is exactly 4 scalars, from `isEmDash` (Text.swift:69-74): U+2014, U+2015, U+2E3A, U+2E3B, each mapped to ASCII "-"; U+2013 en dash is deliberately kept (Text.swift:40). The fast path `mayContainEmDash` (Text.swift:50-65) scans UTF-8 bytes for E2 80 94 / E2 80 95 / E2 B8 BA / E2 B8 BB before walking graphemes. ENGINEERING DECISION correcting the critic: the transform is IDEMPOTENT - after one pass no em dash remains, so `mayContainEmDash` short-circuits and later passes are free no-ops. Running it on the same text twice cannot corrupt it. The real hazard is the opposite one: MISSING a pass, since the read pass exists precisely to clean documents written by builds that only cleaned on arrival (comment at ThreadRuntime.swift:557-561).
resolutions.port_impact: Implement one idempotent helper and call it at all 7 sites. Keep the byte-level prescan - it is a measured optimisation for streaming deltas. Keep the en dash. Do not attempt to deduplicate the passes.

upstream_defects: DroppyCode/App/Runtime/ThreadRuntime.swift:2142-2143 with :3429-3431 - the `.notice` event arm calls `appendNotice(notice.level, notice.message)`, and appendNotice constructs a brand new `Notice(level: level, message: message)`. Every other field of the incoming Notice is silently discarded, in particular `Notice.limit` (Timeline.swift:211). AutoContinue.swift:144-148 sets `notice.limit = LimitNotice(threadID: threadID)` and pushes it through `rehearse(.notice(notice))`; the mark never reaches the timeline item. Effect: the usage-limit notice is stored as a plain `.info` row with no way to identify the thread it belongs to.

DroppyCode/App/Runtime/AutoContinue.swift:83 - `outcomes[threadID] = .handedOff(made.id)` stores the new thread's UUID, and the only reader in the tree (LimitResumeBadge.swift:57) matches `.handedOff` without binding it. The payload is write-only dead data.

DroppyCode/App/Runtime/ThreadRuntime.swift:1159-1167 - the three deferral exits in `startTurn` call `enqueueFollowUp(text:attachments:)` and therefore DISCARD the `hydraHeads` and `hydraBrief` parameters. A head's report or a lead's brief that arrives while the runtime is busy, reverting or archived comes back out of the queue as an ordinary user bubble, losing its pill rendering and its heads attribution.

DroppyCode/App/Runtime/ThreadRuntime.swift:1163 - `guard let app, let initialThread = app.thread(threadID), let project = app.project(initialThread.projectID) else { return }` returns WITHOUT enqueueing, unlike the guards on either side of it. A send issued while the thread or its project is momentarily unresolvable is dropped with no notice and no queue entry.

DroppyCode/App/Runtime/ThreadRuntime.swift:1380-1392 - `warmSession` leaves `warmup` holding a finished Task when `ensureSession` throws (line 1390 clears it only on success). Because line 1381 requires `warmup == nil`, warm starts are permanently disabled for that runtime instance after a single failed start. The comment at 1389 shows the non-retry is intended; the permanent latch reads as a side effect of it rather than a stated goal.

DroppyCode/Core/Support/Text.swift:80 and DroppyCode/App/Runtime/ThreadRuntime.swift:3370 - both comments assert the 200_000 cap is 'the same cap' as the other's, but the two constants bound different operands (input sum vs produced hunk). The comments are wrong; the behaviour is what it is. Reproduce the behaviour, and do not propagate the comments.

DroppyCode/Core/Support/RecentCache.swift:43-46 - `insert` calls `removeValue(for: key)` BEFORE the `guard cost <= costLimit else { return }` check. Inserting an over-budget value for a key that is already cached evicts the existing good entry and stores nothing, leaving the cache worse than before the call.

DroppyCode/Core/Support/RecentCache.swift:47-53 - on rollover the old `previous` map is overwritten by `current` in one assignment; any key that was only in `previous` is dropped without its cost being accounted anywhere except the wholesale `previousCost = currentCost`. This is the intended generational behaviour, but it means the cache can drop a very recently promoted entry at the next rollover.
